game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is my second time round playing this game, and felt it was worthy of a review. Immerse yourself into the world that is Orwell, can you imagine a world in which your every move is observed covertly? The government can find everything about you with a few simple clicks? Orwell is a great game and yet somehow I geniunely felt like I should have been recieving some kind of salary for playing (working). You are the decider, what is relevant and what can we ignore. Sometimes the choice is obvious, in certain cases you geniunely feel like you could have made a mistake. You call the shots. Or do you? 

I am relatively new to gaming so at the moment a games concept is the biggest factor in choosing whether or not to play (I guess that's typical for everyone though) yet for some reason when I first looked into Orwell I thought to myself -  this looks like you're playing as a desky for the government. Basically ya. You are.I can understand those who find it hard to immerse into this game, it's a game of reading and analysing text bu the story and characters are what keep you intrigued. This game is definitely rich in story line and leaves you thinking about the society you live in. Who is watching? What do they know?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL:DR, I myself enjoyed this game, great if you are into detective type work. Not a super exciting but overall 7/10

For the record, I got this while on sale for 5 dollars during steam sales. I see normally priced at 10 and that would be a maybe for buying it. 

So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

It was relatively cheap when I purchased it so I gave it a shot. I am glad that I gave this game a shot because I have not been that engrossed in something in a long time. When I was first playing the game it was basicaly "eh" not bad and I enjoying gathering information. As the game progresses you have to make a more decisions on what information should be taken and if something will be of use or not. During one of the first big I guess "choices" of the game I was so nervous on whether or not I made the correct decision. This game was able to make me feel emotion which really surpised me. At first I just thought it was a little cool but then it became somehting that I had to do. I thought about taking a break but I could not and played through the game in one siting. This one sitting took me about 4 hours and I know that I can play the game a few more times and hopefully have some different outcomes. (only played once so far so...) game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review like all my other reviews, if you want a better full review, then please read better reviews then mine [/h1]

[quote] PLEASE NOTE: This review is being cast as a full review and not a first impressions review because the main bulk of the game is finished, although Orwell does have a story mode, it has different endings and choices, hence, this review is being cast as full because the main bulk of the game is complete, so please, think before you comment! Enjoy :) [/quote]

Orwell is a game developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Surpise Attack Games. Orwell is a compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned. It has an intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode..."

It does have some interesting characters who are easy to become attached to but not for long due to its short story and the game is intellectually satisfying. The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation, basically meaning, it doesn't treat you like an idiot

However, Orwell is a fairly short game, finishing just one story with one ending in 2-3 hours is pretty damn short and currently there are no revising chapters and changing decisions. You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices, however the developers have stated that they will change this in the near future with a patch

Orwell plays similar to a detective visual novel. If you are looking for flashy cutscenes and first/third person character control, then this is not the game for you. You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world. In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story!

Orwell pays homage to one of the greatest writers of all time; George Orwell himself who has created some classic literary works such as Animal Farm and 1984 which this is inspired from!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge. [h1] Cons: [/h1] • Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings. It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game. If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads. If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through. What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat. • *Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent. They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention. If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact. Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified. You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent. • Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload. I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for. The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together. • Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently. Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait. The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before. • Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later. I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile. • It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away. For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information. • Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them. The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with. [h1] Conclusion: [/h1] Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely. Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us. Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force. This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power. A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice. An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction. True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries? We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted. These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion. If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer. Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review. You don't know who could be reading it. It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that. We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right? Oh crap, I hear them at my door. They're on to me! Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-! *Device has been disconnected*

Orwell is a visual novel kind of game that gives you the tools to snoop into people's bank accounts, computers, private conversations and social media sites. You will have to decide which pieces of information are relevant and whether you will reveal your subject's most intimate secrets to the government surveillance program. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: Don't bother, you're basically just a human web-crawler.

This game completely misses the point of what Orwellian infrastructure would look like in the first place and does everything in its power to not allow you any information at all. This game has no right to call itself Orwell, it has nothing to do with surveillance. Yea you have access to data, but the constant opinionated non-rational commentary by the "Adviser" undermines the whole of it. I can't of course claim the outcome wouldn't be the same in an actually Orwellian policy, but it sure as hell shouldn't look like this. In no way am I defending Orwellian values either, but their implementation here is.. well it isn't. It's just not there.
When choose information to be considered, the information changes between the point where you drag it from and the actual information recorded. 
The UI is unintuitive and very hard to navigate. The artificial load times don't help either, from both the gameplay loop and story-telling perspective, they make no sense.

Just to blow of some steam about how disappointed I am in this game, I'll address a couple reviews:

“Grabs the problem of how we balance our own liberty and our safety and turns it into a thrilling adventure.” 9/10 – Polygon
It does make a feeble attempt at tackling the problem of balancing safety and liberty, but fails miserably. Not only does it not represent what you could call Orwellian infrastructure, it doesn't even try. Access to information is limited and the information itself misinterpreted. Your "superior" is clearly opinionated, easily influenced and not of very high deductive capacity. Hardly a "thrilling adventure", the pace of the game is dictated by the game, not by the player. You can't move fast, despite the game making constant remarks about how you should. Nothing about this is thrilling, it's a very slow burner, except it isn't good. It's attempting to show flaws in Orwellian policies but fails to represent them, only showing flaws in its own design.

“A harrowing look into a reality where Big Brother is always watching” Rock Paper Shotgun
The only "harrowing" thing about this game is how it managed to get out of indev. The UI of this game is atrocious in both mechanical as well as logical sense. Mechanically navigating anywhere in this game is a pain in the bum, and the game punishes you every time you try to make more than 1 action per 10 seconds. The whole bit about conflicting data chunks is just stupid. First of all it should have a dating mechanism in the data collection software, which would prevent 90% of the data chunk conflicts in the first place. Secondly, why bother trying to pick one out of the 2 conflicting data points when all you're doing is presenting to someone who can clearly barely tie their own shoe-laces, much less decide outcomes for other people. I wouldn't let this "Adviser" choose the color of desktop background, much less my or anyone else's legal standing. Oh and did I mention: You can't go back on whatever the "Adviser" was saying either, so tough luck if you wanted to submit 2 pieces of information and started navigating before you can notice the Adviser popping up on screen, immediately skipping possibly vital dialog.

“In an age where so much personal information is willingly released by so many, Orwell brilliantly explores the implications of this data being misinterpreted.” 8/10 – GameSpot
This. That's the exact problem with the game, there isn't supposed to be an interpretation to be done in the first place. At the start of the game, you're presented with the job of a data-gatherer. It's not up to you to interpret this data and neither should it be up to the "Adviser". Not just because his brain activity matches that of a fork, but because he simply does not have all the data. Neither does the player, nobody does. Once the information is conclusive all on it's own and only then should there be an attempt at interpretation. It's a simple rational analysis up until then. Or at least it should've been. Instead the game constantly pedals it's own point with forced story-telling.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

review_text_raw: Before buying this game, I saw that most of the top rated reviews just spoke about comparison's to Orwellian works, modern social networks, and Papers Please. And I thought important to address a couple of things after playing through what is available. Orwell is an episodic game; meaning, this is not the final result. This is more of a "Whodunit" than a Thriller mystery, so judging it for linearity might be unfair since they attempt to make you the detective by providing you with a given set of aesthetics. Now talking about aesthetics, this game/experience has its obvious references to Orwell and "1984" -- mainly -- but it is very clear they are only used for inspiration. This is no de facto Orwell Fan Fiction, just an experienced based on some questions the devs had about resembling aspects of society. From the two episodes they have released, I can tell that this is comparable to Papers Please in that you have to provide an analysis to come up with game altering decisions. However, since this is a "Whodunit" type mystery, and are limited to less than half of the intended story arc, we cannot truly make that comparison. What I can say without spoiling, is that there are choices that can either save or spare hundreds of lives, and the deciding factor is actually a juxtaposition of logic I have yet to fully grasp and understand. I think this is a great game; yet, it remains an aesthetic experience we are not yet able to finalise. I look forward for Episode 3's release in three day's time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/-dAXOFIVEDw

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.
