game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]! This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label. What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close. What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game. So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An amazing concept, but the result is disappointing.
1) You do not investigate. You search documents for highlighted clues that you may upload into an investigation database. And you cannot delete them when they turn out to be misleading. Naturally i was careful not to upload dubious claims. Wrong. That gets you stuck. Orwel thrives on rumours, you have to upload these to get new related documents.

2) The writing is boring. The rudimentary gameplay wouldn't matter if the writing was fresh, but the documents you have to go through are as boring as real corporate websites and random people's blogs. Add an annoying coworker and you start regretting you have got that job.

3) The game only pretends to tackle complex issues of privacy and security. The Government is a classical dystopian government that can and will prosecute on "suggestive evidence" which can easily be an off-hand remark of a third party taken out-of-context. If you do not like that, you can side with bomb-throwing anarchists. No third option though, so either way there will be bad outcomes. And that is why surveillance is bad, or so the logic goes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is, as you might guess from the title, a near-future dystopian terrorism thriller told through the lens of the titular national surveillance system of a fictional country called simply The Nation. You learn about the characters through their chat logs, social media and blog posts etcetera and slowly build up a picture of what is going on. But will it be the right picture, or will it lead to more bombings? Will the guilty parties get arrested or will law enforcement focus on the wrong targets? All this and more is up to you, as a faceless "investigator" assigned to the Orwell mass surveillance project.

It looks like it was originally released episodically but it works just as well playing it all the way through. But remember: the system only makes connections based on the data YOU upload to it. If you pick the wrong information, things can go sideways very badly.

I picked this game up in the Christmas 2016 sale and have enjoyed my first playthrough greatly, so I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a story and character driven thriller of this kind. Do be prepared for a lot of clicking, scrolling and dragging and dropping though.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

Very different from Orwell, but masterpieces for me in the revolution in video game design they brought to different elements of the industry.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Given all the positive reviews, I thought Orwell would be a more interesting game than it actually is.
But the gameplay is mostly boring. In a way, it is very similar to a text-adventure game. You read through/listen to all the documents given access to (webpages, chat sessions or phone calls). But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Except most of the info you have to read through is about the different suspects boring life, relationships and habits, things I don't give a damn about. So I guess this game is not for me.

Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

review_text_raw:
If you like games with a lot of actual gameplay this isn't for you. But if you like story-driven, psychological thrillers that keep you guessing, you're in for a treat. 

The UI and art style is extremely crisp and surprisingly uncluttered considering the amount of stuff you constantly have to click through. Articles and conversations are well-written, and the characters have a lot of personality.

The music/sound is minimal, but the game does a great job of using it to increase drama during major discoveries.

Story is really good, by far the highlight of the game. Without spoiling anything, there are lots of twists that you don't really see coming. And I have to say, the game manages to get a lot of emotion into a game with no voice acting. You really do start to feel for some of these characters at times. 

Overall, if you really like this type of game it will be worth $10. It is short (I've beaten it in about 4.5 hours) but it never feels like it's dragging on to the point where I just wish it would end. It's just solid action from start to finish. One of my favorite games of 2016.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A fun little document reading simulator.

Seriously, that is the gameplay. It's like a season of 24, where you have to find out where the bomb is going to go off, and it's all up to you, but instead of an elite anti-terrorist agent, you're some rando sitting in front of a PC, hired to sift through documents. That is literally who you are, in the universe of the game. You submit portions of documents to the system, and this unlocks more documents. That may sound a little silly, but the game explains itself pretty well.

No need to worry about 'pixel hunting' or broken logic - all problems are solved and the plot is progressed in all cases by finding the right entry in the right document. If anything, the game holds your hand. 

You can only submit portions of any document that the system deems potentially relevant. You cannot get a game over - you could play this game through by blindly submitting every bit of highlighted text you found, without paying attention to the plot.

But the plot itself is worth paying attention to - a slow-burn story of a parallel world with technology from five minutes into the future. That lawyer guy on youtube who rates the legal accuracy of various pieces of pop culture would probably not rate this thing too highly. But it is fun, and the rationale for everything that happens is internally consistent.

There are branching paths and different outcomes to minor plot points, as well as alternate endings, depending on how you play  - which boils down to which pieces of information you choose to submit or not submit. It is worth the second and even third play-throughs needed to explore every possible outcome.

Which brings me to my two main complaints:

- There is a checkpoint system, limited to the five main chapters/days of the campaign. You can replay a previous day/chapter, but as soon as you start say, chapter two, your progress in the remaining 3 chapters is lost.

- There is no fast-track buttons for voice or text conversations - they play out in real time, complete with 'realistic' pauses, whether you like it or not.

Neither of these are game-breaking, and are more just quality of life features that I found to be conspicuously absent. Their absence mean that secondary playthroughs for achievements/branch discovery take a little longer than they otherwise would.

I bought Orwell on sale, and went in to it without doing much homework, but I got the impression that this would be several distinct yet related cases. It's more like one big ongoing case. Also in contrast to the Ace Attorney games, which Orwell reminds me of just a little, the plot is a little more serious, and the characters a little less colorful. But if you like that series, or sifting through documents to find a terrorist in a dystopian alternate world sounds like fun to you, and if none of what I have written sounds like a deal-breaker, and you find this game at a price that you think is worth ten or so hours of gameplay, go for it.

One final thought - this game is about a surveillance state, but it doesn't take the easy way out. It poses the dilemma of government overreach/corruption for 'safety' vs. privacy/freedom concerns in an interesting way. I would not say that Orwell is quite as brilliant or profound as some of the glowing reviews suggest, but I do like the way that the plot, the gameplay, and the endings you are able to choose all come together to get you thinking about this issue, even if just a little.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's really hard for me to determine whether I do or don't recommend this, as I'm right on the line. I think overall, though, I have to lean into not recommending it.

The game starts off really well, with a really balanced juxtaposition of people being concerned about privacy versus the very real result of what you're able to accomplish through spying, really highlighting the blurred line between privacy and security. Further, the fact that there are rules in place - such as you can't hack someone without what is essentially a warrant from higher up in the system - makes it feel more grounded, and honestly like a more fair system. 

However, as you reach the end of the game, this completely falls apart. In the closing act, you get beaten around the head with the game designers' opinion, which is a very black-and-white "spying bad, privacy good", which entirely undermines the nuance the entire game up until that point had executed so well. I'll save the spoiler-filled rant for the end.

In addition to this, the gameplay has some glaring flaws. There are certain pieces of information that you absolutely [i]must[/i] collect to move forward, which is sometimes information that seems completely irrelevant (and you're outright told not to submit irrelevant information), forcing you to comb through every possible source with a fine-toothed comb, and sometimes just guess what they want you to submit.

Also, you can only extract verbatim phrases to submit, devoid of any context or clarification. Often, this leads to bizarre interpretations from the game. Like, apparently the game makers think [spoiler]that Depression or PTSD are things that make someone dangerous, rather than being a potentially debilitating disability[/spoiler]. Or perhaps you want to flag one piece of information because of it's context, but because that context isn't part of the auto-selected snippet, the game completely misinterprets it. For example, [spoiler]one girl is in a relationship with a guy, and helps herself to his wallet to make a couple purchases. Any reasonable person would have enough context to say, "Oh, she's borrowing his wallet, and he's only mildly annoyed that she's spending a lot? Clearly they are in a very serious relationship." How about the game? "She took his wallet? She has a history of theft! She's clearly a criminal!"[/spoiler] Like, wtf?

So that's why I just can't recommend this game. Despite the promise it shows, it really undermines itself, especially in the final stretch.

Now, about that endgame rant... Endgame spoilers follow: [spoiler]You reach the end of the game, and basically get lectured at by someone who (1) organized multiple bombings that killed dozens of people, (2) lied to and manipulated multiple friends to do her dirty work, ruining their lives, and (3) is completely unrepentant (going with the "can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs" excuse). What's worse, is that she did all this to protest the whole mass-spying thing, but the only reason you're even spying on anyone in that community is because of the bombings! Literally, she created the problem that she's complaining about.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Meanwhile, you (potentially) used [i]your[/i] minor sin of spying to save dozens or even hundreds of lives at the mall [i]she[/i] tried to bomb - targeting civilians to make people care more about her message. She also blames you for sending police in who end up killing her friend, just because, you know, they actually [i]were[/i] guilty of setting bombs to kill people, and opened fire on the police. How dare those cops return fire on a known bomber who is armed and dangerous just because she shot first![/spoiler]

[spoiler]And what's worse, is that all the other people involved in the plot-device-conference-call at the end [i]take her side![/i] Like, [i]really?[/i] In the end, you're basically pushed to take down the entire system you've been a part of, despite the fact that the game shows it doing an objectively good job of keeping people safe and bringing conspiracies to justice, because spying is bad, just, end of story, just take our word for that.[/spoiler]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game could easily keep one absorbed for hours. It doesn't mess about and places you slap bang in the middle of an ever expanding conspiracy, ramping up the tension and forcing you to act. You will be forced to reason and employ sound logic to get through, with each decision you make raising the stakes even further. With no way to reverse the decisions you've made, you better hope you've made the right ones.

Having played this game up to the conclusion of the second chapter, I find myself astounded by how quickly the tension in a game can rise when all you're doing is playing around with text. It really is a game that can get the heart racing at points, and you'll find yourself crossing your fingers and waiting in silent anticipation as you see the results of your actions unfold. A truly thrilling experience, with fantastic scope for expansion in the future and the occasionally subtle Orwell reference thrown in for those familiar with the (loose) source material.

Definitely one I'd recommend.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Thanks to the recent sale on narrative games and my watching Oreimo for the first time (Do not ask about the correlation) I decided to pick up this game as there is little more fascinating to me than dystopian scenarios and a good mystery story - which is of course what we have right here otherwise I wouldn't be talking about it.

While I am not one to preach about privacy issues in real society this game offers a powerful insight into where things go wrong, even when it seems all the necessary precautions are being made to keep privacy invasion to a minimum. The core concept sees you working for the government of a fictitious foreign nation which has introduced numerous security systems and laws in order to reduce crime levels. While this is all well and good in theory it fails to stop a terrorist attack taking place in plain view of the entire nation. Your task - and there is no choice but to accept it - is to investigate the suspicious individuals linked with these attacks by searching through their social media, medical documents, online dating accounts - literally any source of digital information in which small chunks of information can be uploaded to the government in order to draw conclusions.

What those conclusions are however is often up to you, while the game does a very good job of using all its various information sources to lead you to the right chunks of data conflicts do arise. When a chunk of data contradicts with another it is up to you to decide which side of the argument you wish to submit. You can draw a conclusion quickly, or use all the information at your disposal to logically determine which is correct - simple though it sounds there are instances where no amount of logic will lead to the answer, the choice is then left to your conscience, and which choice you believe is the right one to make. Take note that the game makes no attempt to hide the fact that you are affecting real (fictional) lives and the implications of your actions will very quickly become apparent - People will almost certainly die because of things that you have done, or that you did not do.

Before I continue rambling about the core concept of this game and how powerful it is and how exciting it is to slowly unravel the mystery at the heart of things though, I do have to comment on probably the one thing that really stood out to me  - [b]Sound[/b]
Yes it is weird to comment about how powerful sound is when you play a 6 hour game that for almost its entirety is the same slow jingle of ambient generic "We are a megacorporation" music, there was never a point in the game where i wasn't drastically unsettled by the sudden, VERY powerful changes in this music that occurred the few times where a huge piece of key information is displayed on the screen for the first time. Your eyes might not even be there yet, you might still be reading the paragraph above and just preemptively scrolled the page down already but BOOM, the music plays, something big is right there in front of you, highlighted in blue and in plain view. Your eyes aren't there yet but you know it is there. You want to finish reading the paragraph above for full context, but it's right there. You know it is there. You must look. You must.

TL;DR: Powerful game, intriguing mystery afoot, definitely recommend, please play with sound

10/10 Would invade your privacy again, no matter the cost - Good thing there's a sequel

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've never actually made a review for a game before, but as I got the last achievement(which I did in only - I think - three games I own) and finished the game for like the fourth time, I think a positive review is mandatory. 

God, I love this game.

I'm a fan of these "political simulators" as I've seen these kinds of games adressed as, those where the player works for the government/media or some other important institution and makes decisions that later change the lives of the characters around them in various ways.

In this game, you play as an investigator for a nation-wide surveillance program, in which you have to collect information on potentially dangerous(according to your superiors at least) people and put them into a system, based on which the people above you then act(I suppose it's kind of a bad description, but whatever), and it's probably the best game of it's kind for me, though people might be inclined to disagree.

Orwell required some logical thinking, but not to a degree it was difficult, which I liked - I had to think about it, but I wouldn't get lost in it. I liked the characters, they were fun, none of them was obnoxious to me(some find the advisor - the character of your coworker, that at first guides you through the game and to who you forward your chosen information you find - very obnoxious, but for me, he was the best character, honestly), and I liked seeing the details, or bigger things change based on the choices I made in various routes.

I'd say the game has some replay value - if just to see the three more endings you didn't get on the first try, or to change  the fates of some characters who's lives you directly influenced through your actions.

It's a text based game, so I wouldn't recommend it to people who don't like to read much while playing games, but I think that's obvious from the pictures, videos, maybe even premise...

There's one thing I could think of critiquing right now, which is that when you're listening to people's phone calls or reading their texts in the game, at least to me it's lengthy even if you have the speed of those things set to the highest, mainly during replays.

I'm not sure if I'd buy it for ten euros though - I bought this game on sale, but then again, I bought almost all the games I own on Steam during a sale. If I think about it... I'd probably buy it for the full price now, knowing just how much I liked it, but if you aren't completely sure you're going to love it, I would probably wait for a sale. But maybe I just don't like spending too much money on Steam, since the price isn't even THAT high if I look at it transcribed to my country's currency.

Overall, I can say that I enjoyed Orwell very much, it's one of my most favorite games of all time, even if it might not be one of the objectively best games I played, it is one of the best for me, and I'd recommend it to anyone who would ask.

review_text_raw:
The premise of searching through social media to uncover a hidden group brought me to this game. When I was playing it though the structure of the game felt off to me, there was too little freedom to discover for myself the conspiracy that was going on. Certain necessary options are highlighted beforehand, so that skimming (or even skipping) the text was an option. Any puzzle/detective game that is as on-rails as this one is bound to lack any critical reasoning.

Also the use of Orwellian politics is so reductive that it almost entirely avoids any real political discussion (bad State controls people, we need "freedom", whatever that is).

My advice is that if you want political commentary then read a book instead. If you want a good detective story then read a book instead. Either way I'd rather read a book than play this game any day,

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though. Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope. This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.
